paragraphs: This paper examines how a graph neural network’s internal features change when it learns to classify nodes. Its starting point is neural collapse: in classifiers trained beyond zero training error, examples from the same class develop increasingly similar final features, while class averages approach symmetric arrangements. The authors ask how graph connections affect this behavior.

An empirical study, illustrated through community detection on stochastic block model graphs, finds that features within a class also become less variable in node classification. However, this contraction is weaker than in the instance classification setting. The theoretical analysis shows that even an optimistic mathematical model needs a strict condition on graph structure to admit a minimizing solution with exact collapse.

The authors also examine the model’s gradient dynamics to explain the partial collapse observed experimentally. A further study tracks variation within and between classes across a trained GNN’s layers and compares it with spectral methods. Together, these results connect feature geometry to graph topology and explain why collapse behavior from ordinary classifiers does not carry over unchanged.
neurips-2023-a-neural-collapse-perspecti.tldr: Graph structure constrains neural collapse in GNNs, helping explain why same-class node features become similar without necessarily collapsing completely.

paragraphs: Transfer attacks construct adversarial examples using a source model and then apply them to a different target model. Their practical appeal is that an attacker can work through the surrogate without directly using the target to construct the examples. This paper asks why such examples transfer, seeking a quantitative account that brings together previously separate empirical explanations.

The authors introduce the manifold attack model as a unified theoretical framework. It formalizes common intuitions about transferability and accounts for existing empirical observations. One result explains how attacks can transfer even when the source model is inaccurate, showing that source prediction accuracy alone does not explain the phenomenon within this framework.

The model also links the existence of transferable adversarial examples to the curvature of the data manifold—the geometry of how data are arranged. This relationship offers a quantitative explanation for the difficulty of increasing transfer attack success rates. The paper discusses the model’s expressive power and possible extensions, positioning it as an explanatory framework rather than a universal account established for every application.
neurips-2023-a-theory-of-transfer-based-.tldr: A manifold-based theory explains adversarial transferability and connects the existence of transferable attacks to data geometry.

paragraphs: Time series forecasting becomes difficult when the statistical properties of a sequence change over time. Normalization can reduce this variation, but existing approaches often treat an entire input sequence as statistically uniform. They can also overlook differences between the observed sequence and the future interval being predicted. This paper addresses both issues through slice-level adaptive normalization, or SAN.

SAN operates on local sections of a sequence rather than applying one statistical treatment to the whole instance. This makes normalization more flexible when different parts of the input have different properties. A separate lightweight network models how the raw series’ statistical properties evolve, supporting adaptive normalization and the corresponding conversion of predictions back to their original scale.

The framework is designed as a model-agnostic plugin, and the authors instantiate it with four widely used forecasting models on benchmark datasets. Its central contribution is to make changing local statistics an explicit part of forecasting. The evaluation investigates its effectiveness, while additional analyses examine how the proposed normalization approach behaves.
neurips-2023-adaptive-normalization-for-.tldr: SAN normalizes local time-series slices and models evolving statistics to help forecasting models handle changing data distributions.

paragraphs: A vision model can make choices similar to a person’s without explaining how long that person takes to decide. This paper examines that temporal dimension of alignment. It develops a methodology for deriving a reaction-time measure from a model that processes visual stimuli and has been optimized for a task.

The proposed metric draws on subjective logic theory to summarize evidence accumulation in recurrent vision models. Recurrence provides a sequence of internal processing steps, giving the method something to analyze beyond the final choice. The goal is to connect the model’s evolving evidence with patterns of decision timing, making reaction time part of the computational account of visual behavior.

The authors demonstrate alignment with human reaction-time patterns under stimulus manipulations across four tasks, spanning perceptual grouping, mental simulation, and scene categorization. These findings support using the metric to study temporal similarities between model and human strategies. The proposed broader value is a route toward testable neuroscience hypotheses in additional cognitive tasks, rather than an established explanation of timing across all visual behavior.
neurips-2023-computing-a-human-like-reac.tldr: An evidence-accumulation metric from recurrent vision models aligns with human reaction-time patterns across four visual tasks.

paragraphs: Counting cycles is a useful test of whether a graph neural network can recognize meaningful graph structure. Many models with proven counting abilities extract and process collections of subgraphs, which brings substantial preprocessing, memory, and computation costs. This paper develops an alternative based on the pair-processing FWL(2) graph algorithm.

The proposed d-DRFWL(2) networks restrict message passing to node pairs separated by at most distance d. This retains a way to reason about relationships between pairs while exploiting graph sparsity and avoiding expensive subgraph extraction. The distance parameter provides a means to balance expressive power against computational complexity.

The main theoretical result is that setting d to just two still permits counting every cycle of lengths three, four, five, and six. Six-membered cycles are especially relevant to molecular graphs, including benzene rings. Experiments on synthetic and molecular datasets support the theory. The authors also report that, to their knowledge, the distance-two model is the most efficient model then available with this six-cycle counting capability, both theoretically and empirically.
neurips-2023-distance-restricted-folklor.tldr: Restricting pairwise graph message passing to nearby nodes preserves provable counting of three- through six-cycles while reducing computational costs.

paragraphs: DSR models protein motion through a continuous representation of the protein’s surface in space and time. The approach uses a neural network to represent a signed distance function, whose zero-valued locations define the surface. Including time in this representation lets the same model describe how that surface changes as the protein moves.

This formulation supports evaluating the representation across spatial locations and times, rather than limiting the description to separate surface snapshots. The authors report that their model accurately captures protein trajectories and can interpolate and extrapolate in both space and time. They describe the work as the first successful application of this approach to large-scale protein dynamics.

The surface representation also simplifies calculations used to identify movement directions and amplitudes of protein domains. This connects the learned geometry to quantities useful for studying protein motion. The paper presents DSR as a promising, more scalable and efficient alternative to existing first-principles and deep learning approaches, with its experimental results supporting the proposed representation’s usefulness for dynamics research.
neurips-2023-dsr-dynamical-surface-repre.tldr: DSR represents moving protein surfaces with neural signed distance functions, enabling continuous modeling and analysis across space and time.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows clients to contribute to a shared model, but their data can come from substantially different distributions. This paper identifies a problem inside the learned representations: local training can bias features toward a client’s domain and weaken their more general usefulness. The authors call this loss of generic feature quality representation degeneration.

Their Domain Bias Eliminator, or DBE, is a general framework for addressing the problem in representation space. Its theoretical analysis connects reduced discrepancy between server and client representations with improved knowledge transfer in both directions. The intended benefit is therefore shared: clients can contribute useful knowledge to the server while also benefiting from what the server has learned.

Experiments on four datasets show substantial improvements when DBE is added to existing federated learning methods, covering both generalization and personalization. The authors also report that a DBE-equipped method outperforms ten state-of-the-art personalized federated learning methods by a large margin. These findings support treating representation mismatch as a useful intervention point when clients have statistically heterogeneous data.
neurips-2023-eliminating-domain-bias-for.tldr: DBE reduces server–client representation mismatch to improve knowledge transfer, generalization, and personalization in federated learning.

paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks can model aspects of the visual system, yet strong task performance does not automatically explain properties of the primary visual cortex, V1. The paper focuses on neural properties associated with biological circuitry that remain inadequately explained by models trained with adversarial examples or extensive data augmentation.

The authors systematically add neuroscience-inspired architectural components to task-trained CNNs. These components simulate center-surround antagonism, local receptive fields, tuned normalization, and cortical magnification. The aim is to determine which mechanisms help the networks’ internal representations account for V1 activity and tuning, making biological structure part of the model design.

The resulting models achieve state-of-the-art explanation of V1 neural activity and tuning properties in the reported evaluation. Analyses of learned component parameters and stimuli that maximally activate network neurons provide additional support for the components’ explanatory roles. The findings establish a useful set of architectural mechanisms for modeling V1, while the broader prospect of advancing neuroscience and AI through increasingly accurate computational brain models remains a potential implication.
neurips-2023-explaining-v1-properties-wi.tldr: Adding specific biologically inspired components to CNNs improves their explanation of V1 neural activity and tuning properties.

paragraphs: FineMoGen addresses a gap in text-driven motion generation: producing plausible movement is easier than following instructions that specify detailed spatial and temporal actions. The framework uses diffusion modeling to generate and edit motion with finer control over how actions are composed across space and time.

Its central architectural contribution is Spatio-Temporal Mixture Attention, or SAMI. This transformer architecture explicitly models constraints on spatial and temporal composition when constructing its global attention template. It also uses a sparsely activated mixture of experts to extract detailed features adaptively. These two mechanisms connect instruction structure with the features used during motion generation.

The authors introduce HuMMan-MoGen to support study of the task, containing 2,968 videos and 102,336 detailed spatial and temporal descriptions. Experiments report better motion generation quality than state-of-the-art methods. With assistance from large language models, FineMoGen also supports zero-shot motion editing that follows fine-grained instructions. The contribution therefore combines a generation architecture, a dataset, and an editing capability aimed at more precise user control.
neurips-2023-finemogen-fine-grained-spat.tldr: FineMoGen combines diffusion and specialized attention to generate and edit motion from detailed spatial and temporal instructions.

paragraphs: Down-sampling reduces the spatial size of image representations and is a standard operation in neural networks. This paper revisits common approaches and identifies biased effects associated with static weighting strategies. FouriDown reformulates down-sampling in the Fourier domain so that the weighting operation can be learned and adapted to context.

The method organizes corresponding frequency positions into a channel dimension, then shuffles channels according to whether their frequency bins are susceptible to aliasing. This arrangement is intended to keep weight learning consistent. The complete operator combines a two-dimensional Fourier transform, context-dependent shuffling, adaptive weighted superposition, and an inverse Fourier transform.

The approach provides a unified formulation of existing down-sampling techniques while introducing a more flexible operator that can be integrated into image restoration networks. Experiments on image deblurring and low-light enhancement consistently show significant performance improvements. The findings support changing how frequency information is organized and combined during down-sampling as a useful way to improve these restoration tasks.
neurips-2023-fouridown-factoring-down-sa.tldr: FouriDown makes down-sampling learnable and context-adaptive through frequency-domain shuffling and weighted combination.

paragraphs: This paper explores a simpler way to combine visual and language information without relying on expensive fine-tuning of increasingly large models. It brings together features from pretrained neural networks and freely available explicit semantic knowledge. The challenge is that some of this external knowledge may be irrelevant to the images being analyzed.

The proposed solution is an implicit, differentiable out-of-distribution detection layer that removes poorly matching knowledge. It performs outlier detection by finding fixed points of a differentiable function and uses the solver’s last iterate for backpropagation. This makes knowledge filtering compatible with the gradient-based training process rather than leaving it as an entirely separate decision.

The authors evaluate the approach on visual question answering, visual reasoning, and image–text retrieval across different datasets. Their experiments show that models built this way can perform similarly to state-of-the-art systems while using significantly fewer samples and less training time. The result supports combining pretrained features with filtered explicit knowledge as a practical approach to the evaluated multimodal tasks.
neurips-2023-implicit-differentiable-out.tldr: A differentiable outlier-detection layer filters external knowledge, enabling efficient multimodal models with performance similar to state-of-the-art systems.

paragraphs: This paper revisits objective perturbation as a method for training models with differential privacy. Its motivation is that differentially private stochastic gradient descent, or DP-SGD, has become the more popular choice, but its versatility comes with costs that may be substantial for simple learners such as linear and logistic regression.

The authors identify two relevant costs: the privacy overhead of tuning hyperparameters privately and the computational demands of the training procedure. Their contribution combines tighter privacy analyses of objective perturbation with new computational tools. These address both how the method’s privacy protection is assessed and how practically it can be used to train a model.

The reported result is competitive performance with DP-SGD on unconstrained convex generalized linear problems. That scope matters: the paper establishes a renewed case for objective perturbation in this specified class of learning problems. Its practical message is that privacy-preserving training for simpler models can benefit from a method whose analysis and computation are developed specifically for that setting.
neurips-2023-improving-the-privacy-and-p.tldr: Tighter privacy analysis and new computational tools make objective perturbation competitive with DP-SGD for unconstrained convex generalized linear learning.

paragraphs: GANs trained on limited data can suffer when their discriminator overfits, destabilizing the competition that drives image generation. NICE addresses this by introducing adaptive multiplicative noise into the discriminator’s internal features. The theoretical analysis shows that this modulation adaptively reduces the discriminator’s Rademacher complexity, helping control overfitting.

Noise modulation also creates a difficulty: it increases gradient norms, which can make training unstable. NICE therefore adds a consistency constraint requiring the discriminator to behave consistently on the same input under different noise modulations. The authors show that this constraint effectively penalizes first- and second-order gradients of the latent features, counteracting the instability introduced by modulation.

Experiments support both parts of the analysis, showing reduced generalization error and the expected gradient penalization. The method achieves state-of-the-art results in the reported limited-data settings on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and FFHQ, as well as in low-shot generation. Its contribution is the coordinated use of adaptive noise and consistency: one controls discriminator overfitting, while the other stabilizes its effects on training.
neurips-2023-nice-noise-modulated-consis.tldr: NICE combines adaptive discriminator noise with a consistency constraint to reduce GAN overfitting and stabilize training with limited data.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces annotation work by choosing which unlabeled examples should receive labels. In open-set settings, the available pool also contains examples outside the target distribution, which can lead to unproductive selections. Existing approaches often try to select only examples believed to belong to the target distribution and filter everything else out.

This paper argues that exclusive focus on presumed in-distribution examples can constrain learning for both the classifier and the out-of-distribution detector. Progressive Active Learning, or PAL, instead actively selects valuable examples from both groups. It evaluates informativeness together with representativeness and progressively balances presumed in-distribution and out-of-distribution selections in each annotation round.

The goal is to improve the classifier’s ability to handle target examples while also strengthening detection of examples outside that target. Experiments across multiple open-set active learning scenarios demonstrate PAL’s effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art methods. The finding is selective: some out-of-distribution examples can contribute useful learning information, and PAL provides a mechanism for including them in the labeling process.
neurips-2023-not-all-out-of-distribution.tldr: PAL improves open-set active learning by balancing informative, representative examples from both presumed in-distribution and out-of-distribution groups.

paragraphs: Neural approaches to combinatorial optimization can learn to generate a distribution of candidate solutions and gradually improve it through gradient-based training. This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding whether suitable solution generators can combine expressive power, manageable model size, and an optimization landscape without suboptimal stationary points.

The authors give a positive existence result: there are generative models that can represent approximately optimal solutions, use a number of parameters polynomial in input size, and satisfy the stated landscape property. The result covers a broad class of problems, including cut problems, constraint satisfaction, maximum-weight bipartite matching, and the Traveling Salesman Problem. The claim concerns these properties of suitable generators.

The analysis also produces a regularization process for ordinary gradient descent. Theoretical and experimental evidence indicates that it helps with vanishing gradients and escaping bad stationary points. Together, the results provide a framework for studying why learning distributions of solutions can be effective, while connecting that theory to a concrete intervention in the optimization procedure.
neurips-2023-optimizing-solution-sampler.tldr: The paper establishes the existence of compact, expressive combinatorial solution generators with benign landscapes and develops a regularizer that helps gradient optimization.

paragraphs: Personalized prediction often depends on information that is sensitive, protected, self-reported, or costly to collect. Yet people may have little ability to decline disclosure or determine whether personalization helps them. This paper treats those choices as part of the prediction system itself, introducing participatory systems that let individuals opt into personalization when a prediction is made.

The authors provide a model-agnostic learning algorithm for supervised tasks in which personalization uses categorical group attributes. This scope makes the method applicable across underlying prediction models while specifying the kind of personal information it handles. The central design goal is to support consent and help people understand the benefit of sharing information.

An empirical study evaluates participatory systems on clinical prediction tasks against common personalization and imputation approaches. The results show that these systems can facilitate informed consent while improving performance and privacy across all groups that report personal data. The contribution connects user participation with predictive modeling, demonstrating that decisions about disclosure can be incorporated into the operation of a learned classifier.
neurips-2023-participatory-personalizati.tldr: Participatory classifiers let people opt into personalization at prediction time, with reported improvements in performance and privacy for groups sharing data.

paragraphs: In-context learning allows a transformer to use examples in a prompt without changing its weights. This paper asks whether that ability can extend to fundamentally new tasks. The authors investigate linear regression while varying the diversity of tasks used during pretraining, making task variety a central experimental variable.

They observe a task-diversity threshold. Below it, the transformer fails to solve unseen regression tasks and behaves like a Bayesian estimator whose prior is the limited pretraining task distribution. Above it, the transformer substantially outperforms that estimator and behaves more like ridge regression, corresponding to a Gaussian prior that also covers tasks absent from pretraining.

In this regression setting, sufficiently diverse pretraining therefore enables optimal in-context solutions to fundamentally new tasks. The crucial departure is from the Bayes-optimal estimator tied specifically to the pretraining distribution; the ridge-like behavior still has a Bayesian interpretation under a broader prior. The study also examines regularization, capacity, and task structure, highlighting task diversity alongside data and model scale in this concrete example.
neurips-2023-pretraining-task-diversity-.tldr: In linear regression experiments, sufficient pretraining task diversity enables transformers to solve unseen tasks through ridge-like in-context learning.

paragraphs: ReHLine is an optimization algorithm for a family of regularized empirical risk minimization problems. These problems combine a loss measuring fit to training data with regularization and, optionally, linear constraints. The supported losses are convex and piecewise linear-quadratic, allowing the framework to cover several distinct learning tasks.

The method is designed to accommodate different combinations of losses, penalties, and constraints within one solver. Examples include FairSVM, elastic-net quantile regression, and Huber minimization. The authors prove a linear convergence rate and show that computation per iteration grows linearly with sample size. These are separate advantages: one concerns optimization progress, while the other concerns the cost of each iteration.

The implementation provides Python and R interfaces. Benchmarks report substantially better computational efficiency than generic optimization solvers on large datasets, along with improvements over specialized solvers for SVM, Huber, and smoothed-SVM tasks. The practical contribution is a flexible solver that retains strong efficiency within its supported problem class, reducing the need to choose between generality and task-specific optimization tools.
neurips-2023-rehline-regularized-composi.tldr: ReHLine efficiently solves a flexible class of convex learning problems with proven linear convergence and iteration costs linear in sample size.

paragraphs: MRI acquires measurements in the spatial Fourier domain. Efficient non-Cartesian sampling trajectories, such as spirals, use longer readouts but are more vulnerable to magnetic field variations. These variations produce off-resonance artifacts, including image blurring. ResoNet addresses that blur using the accurate physical model of how it arises.

The framework trains exclusively on synthetic, noise-like data with representative marginal statistics. Training randomizes images, coil sensitivities, and field maps, allowing the network to learn reversal of off-resonance effects from simulated acquisition conditions. The authors report that the resulting model works across diverse anatomies and image contrasts without retraining. It also supports fat/water separation and is compatible with parallel imaging acceleration.

Results on phantom and in-vivo data demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The method’s significance is that a physics-based description of the artifact supports learning from synthetic randomized data rather than requiring training examples for each anatomy and contrast. The authors identify improved clinical adoption of non-Cartesian acquisition, and consequently efficient, rapid, motion-robust scanning, as a potential downstream benefit.
neurips-2023-resonet-noise-trained-physi.tldr: ResoNet learns MRI off-resonance correction entirely from synthetic noise-like data and works across anatomies and contrasts without retraining.

paragraphs: This paper revisits adversarial training on ImageNet, where understanding has lagged behind studies of ResNets and lower-resolution datasets. It compares vision transformers with ConvNeXt convolutional networks in the context of debate about their robustness. The focus includes both resistance to attacks seen during training and generalization to different attack types.

Extensive experiments show that relatively small architectural and training changes can substantially affect robustness. Replacing PatchStem with ConvStem is particularly influential. The changes improve robustness within the training-time l-infinity threat model and produce even larger improvements in generalization to previously unseen l-one and l-two attacks.

The strongest architecture depends on which robustness outcome is being measured. Modified ConvNeXt models with ConvStem achieve the best l-infinity robustness across the evaluated parameter and computation ranges, while vision transformers with ConvStem generalize best to unseen threat models. These findings make architectural details and training choices central to the comparison, showing that broad model-family labels alone do not capture the reported robustness differences.
neurips-2023-revisiting-adversarial-trai.tldr: Small architecture and training changes substantially improve ImageNet adversarial robustness, with different models leading on trained and unseen attack types.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using an unlabeled stream of test data to cope with distribution shifts. This paper examines what happens when that stream also contains noisy or unexpected samples. The authors find that existing methods can deteriorate because they adapt indiscriminately to incoming examples, including samples that should not drive their updates.

Screening-out Test-Time Adaptation, or SoTTA, addresses the problem at two levels. High-confidence uniform-class sampling reduces the influence of noisy inputs. Entropy-sharpness minimization addresses the model parameters, improving their robustness to large gradients caused by noisy samples. Together, the mechanisms control both which data influence adaptation and how sensitive the resulting updates are.

Evaluations on standard adaptation benchmarks include several noisy scenarios. SoTTA outperforms state-of-the-art methods when noisy samples are present and achieves comparable accuracy when they are absent. These results support treating the reliability of the adaptation stream as part of the learning problem, with input screening and parameter robustness working together to protect continual updates.
neurips-2023-sotta-robust-test-time-adap.tldr: SoTTA combines input screening and parameter robustness to improve test-time adaptation on streams containing noisy samples.

paragraphs: Neural signed distance functions represent shapes implicitly, and training commonly uses an eikonal loss to encourage the required distance-function behavior. This paper analyzes a source of instability in that optimization. As network representation power increases, the training dynamics approach an unstable partial differential equation in the continuum limit.

The authors show that this instability can appear in existing network optimization as surface irregularities or convergence to suboptimal local minima, interfering with fine geometry and topology. Some previously used loss terms can eliminate the instability, but they can also smooth away useful detail through excessive regularization. StEik introduces a new regularizer based on the same continuum analysis to counter instability without that over-regularization.

With stability guaranteed in the continuum limit, the authors also investigate a more expressive architecture built from quadratic layers. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that the proposed regularizer and network recover finer shape detail and more accurate topology than existing state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects an analytical diagnosis of training dynamics to both the loss design and the network structure.
neurips-2023-steik-stabilizing-the-optim.tldr: StEik analyzes instability in eikonal-loss training and introduces stabilization and quadratic layers that improve fine shape reconstruction.

paragraphs: Predict+Optimize trains a prediction model with the downstream optimization problem in mind. The goal is for predicted parameters to produce good decisions when judged using the true parameters. This paper addresses the case where unknown quantities appear in constraints, extending beyond the more commonly studied setting where uncertainty affects only the objective.

Earlier work had adapted the framework to uncertain constraints, but its training algorithm covered only covering and packing linear programs. The authors introduce Two-Stage Predict+Optimize as a simpler, more powerful framework and provide a training algorithm usable for all mixed integer linear programs. This substantially broadens the class of constrained decision problems that the approach can address.

Experimental results report superior prediction performance over the classical and state-of-the-art methods included in the evaluation. The paper’s central contribution is the expanded framework and algorithmic applicability: learning can account for downstream optimization even when predicted quantities enter constraints in mixed integer problems. The authors also propose their framework as a canonical formulation, which is a recommendation about how to organize this setting.
neurips-2023-two-stage-predict-optimize-.tldr: Two-Stage Predict+Optimize extends decision-aware prediction to unknown constraint parameters with a training algorithm applicable to all mixed integer linear programs.

paragraphs: Pretrained representations can be useful on new datasets, but their usefulness does not establish whether accompanying uncertainty estimates also transfer. The Uncertainty-aware Representation Learning benchmark, or URL, evaluates both properties. It introduces a metric for measuring zero-shot transfer of uncertainty alongside the transferability of the representations themselves.

The authors apply the benchmark to ten uncertainty quantification methods pretrained on ImageNet and transferred to eight downstream datasets. This setup tests whether uncertainty remains informative when the model is used beyond its original training setting. It therefore adds a reliability dimension to evaluation of pretrained features.

The reported comparison favors methods that model uncertainty in the representation itself or directly estimate prediction risk over methods based on probabilities for the original training classes. Transferable uncertainty nevertheless remains an open challenge. The findings also suggest that improving it need not conflict with conventional representation learning goals. URL provides a way to evaluate that relationship explicitly and guide development of pretrained models with useful features and uncertainty estimates.
neurips-2023-url-a-representation-learni.tldr: URL benchmarks transferable representations and uncertainty, finding advantages for representation-based uncertainty and direct risk estimates.

paragraphs: Voicebox is a text-guided speech generation model trained to fill in speech using surrounding audio and text. It uses non-autoregressive flow matching and is trained on more than 50,000 hours of speech without filtering or enhancement. The infilling task provides a shared training basis for multiple speech generation and editing uses.

The model can learn from context at inference time and can condition on future audio as well as earlier context. Its supported tasks include zero-shot text-to-speech within and across languages, noise removal, content editing, style conversion, and generation of diverse samples. These capabilities make the model a general-purpose approach to several speech tasks.

In the reported zero-shot text-to-speech comparison, Voicebox improves on VALL-E in intelligibility and audio similarity. Word error rate falls from 5.9% to 1.9%, and the audio similarity score rises from 0.580 to 0.681, with generation up to twenty times faster. The results connect a broad infilling-based formulation with both task versatility and strong performance in the stated synthesis comparison.
neurips-2023-voicebox-text-guided-multil.tldr: Voicebox uses large-scale speech infilling to support multilingual synthesis and editing, outperforming VALL-E in the reported zero-shot synthesis comparison.
